reference.source: Apley & Solomon / standard sports medicine references
clinicalPearls: Presents as gradually worsening, activity-related localised bone pain that eases with rest, typically after a change or increase in training load

Fatigue fractures occur when normal bone is subjected to repetitive abnormal load, whereas insufficiency fractures occur when normal load acts on weakened bone such as osteoporotic or pathological bone
Common sites include the metatarsals (march fracture), tibia, navicular, and femoral neck, with the tibia most frequent in runners
Focal bony tenderness, pain on hopping or percussion, and pain reproduced by loading the bone support the diagnosis
Early plain radiographs are often normal, and MRI or bone scan is more sensitive for detecting bone stress injury

Certain high-risk sites, including the tension side of the femoral neck, anterior tibial cortex, navicular, and base of the fifth metatarsal, are prone to non-union or completion and need protected weight-bearing or surgical referral
Management of low-risk fractures is relative rest, activity modification, and graduated return to loading once pain-free
In female athletes consider the female athlete triad / relative energy deficiency in sport, with attention to energy availability, menstrual function, and bone health
Recurrent or multiple stress fractures warrant assessment for metabolic bone disease, vitamin D deficiency, and endocrine causes
reference.pathophysiology: A stress fracture develops when repetitive submaximal loading causes microdamage to accumulate faster than bone can remodel and repair it. Osteoclastic resorption temporarily outpaces osteoblastic formation, weakening the cortex and, if loading continues, progressing from a stress reaction to a frank fracture line. Fatigue fractures reflect excessive load on normal bone, while insufficiency fractures reflect normal load on abnormally weak bone.
additionalDifferentials: Osteoid osteoma or other bone tumour
Pathological fracture from metastasis or metabolic bone disease
additionalInvestigations: Plain radiographs, recognising they are frequently normal early and may show periosteal reaction or a fracture line later
MRI as the preferred sensitive test to grade bone marrow oedema and confirm the fracture
Radionuclide bone scan as an alternative sensitive investigation
CT for suspected navicular or other fractures needing detailed cortical assessment
Metabolic and endocrine workup, vitamin D, and bone density assessment in recurrent, atypical, or insufficiency fractures
redFlags: High-risk sites such as the femoral neck (especially tension side), anterior tibia, tarsal navicular, and fifth metatarsal base that risk non-union or displacement
Groin or hip pain with weight-bearing suggesting femoral neck stress fracture requiring urgent assessment
Features of pathological or insufficiency fracture such as minimal trauma, older age, or known malignancy
Systemic symptoms or signs suggesting infection or tumour
reference.prognosis: Low-risk stress fractures generally heal fully within six to twelve weeks with load modification and graded return, whereas high-risk fractures may progress to non-union or complete fracture and can require prolonged protection or surgery.
pitfalls: Excluding a stress fracture on the basis of a normal early radiograph
Failing to recognise high-risk sites and continuing loading with risk of completion or non-union
Overlooking relative energy deficiency in sport or metabolic bone disease in recurrent cases
Returning to full training too early before the bone has healed
references: Apley & Solomon's System of Orthopaedics and Fractures
management: Relative rest and load modification, reducing the offending repetitive activity to allow remodelling to catch up with microdamage
Protected weight-bearing with a walking boot or crutches for painful lower-limb fractures
Analgesia with paracetamol for pain control
Graded, progressive return to activity once pain-free, correcting training errors and biomechanical factors
Surgical referral and fixation for high-risk sites prone to non-union, including the tension-side femoral neck, anterior tibial cortex, navicular and base of the fifth metatarsal
Assess and optimise bone health and energy availability, checking vitamin D, calcium and bone density and addressing relative energy deficiency in recurrent or insufficiency fractures
Physiotherapy for rehabilitation and prevention of recurrence
